texto: It is seven in the morning. You walk into the kitchen,
and there they are again. A perfect line of tiny ants,
marching from a crack by the window, straight to the sugar bowl.
So you do what everyone does.
You squish them. All of them. Thumb, paper towel,
done. By lunch, the line is back. Same crack.
Same sugar bowl.
So what actually happens to the colony when you squish the ants on your counter?
And why does it never work? The short answer is,
the ants you see are not the colony.
Not even close. First, how did they find your
sugar in the first place? One scout wandered out,
found it, and walked home, dragging her belly on
the counter to leave an invisible scent trail.
Every ant that follows the trail and finds food adds more scent.
So the trail gets stronger and stronger.
Think of it like a food delivery app. The order is on the screen,
and the drivers just follow the map.
Squishing a few drivers does not cancel the order. The map is still there,
and the restaurant sends more.
And the restaurant is huge.
In some ant species, scientists have counted the foragers, and found
they are only seven to fifteen percent of all the workers.
In many species, the ones sent outside are
the older workers, near the end of their lives. To the colony,
they are the most expendable.
Meanwhile, deep inside your wall, there are nurses, builders,
baby ants, and the queen. Sometimes many queens.
So when you squish twenty ants on the counter,
the colony barely notices.
Now, here is a weird test. Next time, smell your fingers.
If it smells like rotten coconut, you just met
the odorous house ant, one of the most common kitchen ants in America.
That smell comes from defensive chemicals
in its body. And to other ants, chemicals like that
can mean danger.
And here is where it gets worse. Say you lose
patience and blast the line with bug spray.
With some house ants, a fast-acting spray can make
the colony do something strange. It splits.
A few queens and a crowd of workers pack up and move out,
and start new nests somewhere else.
Odorous house ants are famous for this. One colony in your wall
can quietly turn into three. And since they are all relatives,
they do not fight each other. They just share
your kitchen.
So what happens to the ants you squished? Their sisters come and carry them away.
In the nineteen fifties, the famous ant
scientist E. O. Wilson figured out how they know
a nestmate is dead. A dead ant gives off a
fatty acid called oleic acid. Ants smell it,
and haul the body to the colony trash pile.
His team even reported that a living ant, painted with that acid,
got carried out to the trash, kicking and very much
alive.
So what actually works? First, wipe the trail with soapy water.
That erases the map, so new ants cannot follow it.
Then put the sugar in a sealed jar.
No order, no delivery.
And if they keep coming, use a slow ant bait instead of spray.
The workers carry it home and share it mouth to mouth,
all the way to the queens. That is how you reach
the colony you never see.
So the next time you see that perfect line on your counter,
remember what you are looking at. Not the army. Just a few delivery drivers,
following a map. Erase the map,
and close the restaurant.
